name: technical-notes
licence: Synthetic, written for this project. Freely reusable.
purpose: A small, fully synthetic corpus of the kind of technical English MetaBare indexes: terminal output, cloud console errors, infrastructure notes. Used to sanity-check candidate text embedding models. It is deliberately NOT a relevance benchmark: 24 documents cannot separate models that differ by a few points on MTEB. It exists to catch a model that is obviously wrong for this domain, and to measure operational characteristics on realistic technical text.
warning: Contains no real account identifiers, hostnames, credentials or personal data. Every value is invented.

documents.text:
$ terraform destroy
Error: deleting EC2 Subnet (subnet-0abc123): DependencyViolation: The subnet 'subnet-0abc123' has dependencies and cannot be deleted.
status code: 400

The load balancer controller left an orphaned network interface behind. Delete the ENI manually, then re-run destroy.

Karpenter did not provision a node for the pending pod. The NodeClaim stayed in Unknown for eleven minutes.

kubectl get nodeclaims
NAME            TYPE   ZONE   READY   AGE
default-x7k2q   -      -      Unknown 11m

Root cause: the subnet had no free IP addresses left. The /27 CIDR was far too small once each pod took an ENI secondary address.

Spot interruption notice received. The instance metadata endpoint returned a termination time two minutes ahead.

curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/instance-action
{"action": "terminate", "time": "2026-05-02T14:22:00Z"}

The node drained cleanly and the in-flight batch went back on the queue. No work was lost, but the visibility timeout had to be longer than the drain.

DocumentDB refused to build the index. The collection had documents whose indexed field exceeded the key size limit.

MongoServerError: index key too large for index entry

Shortening the field to a hash of its value fixed it. Worth remembering that DocumentDB is not MongoDB and its limits differ.

The NAT Gateway was the single largest line on the bill. Thirty-five dollars a month in eu-west-1 before a byte of data was processed, for a workload that mostly talked to S3.

An S3 gateway endpoint is free. Switching the traffic to it removed the need for the gateway entirely in the development environment.

CPUUtilization on the writer instance sat at 94 percent for the whole window. The read replica was almost idle at 6 percent.

CloudWatch showed the imbalance clearly across the two-week range. Nothing was routing reads to the replica because the application used the cluster endpoint for everything.

Pod stuck in ImagePullBackOff.

kubectl describe pod api-7d9f
Failed to pull image: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to pull and unpack image: unexpected status: 401 Unauthorized

The node role had no ecr:GetAuthorizationToken permission. Adding the managed policy to the node instance profile resolved it.

The GPU node took four minutes and ten seconds to go from a pending pod to a first successful inference. The inference itself took eight hundred milliseconds.

Most of the four minutes was the container image pull. The image was six gigabytes because it carried CUDA wheels the model never used.

kubectl get pods -n kube-system
NAME                       READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
coredns-5d78c9869d-4kqxz   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   7          12m

CoreDNS could not start because the cluster had no schedulable node with enough memory. Everything else in the cluster failed in confusing ways downstream of that.

S3 lifecycle transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cost more than it saved. The objects averaged eleven kilobytes, and the per-object transition charge dominated the storage saving.

The minimum billable object size for the class is 128 KB, so each small object was billed as if it were 128 KB anyway.

Prometheus disk filled up. The time series database had grown to forty gigabytes while the application data it was observing was under two gigabytes.

Retention was set to fifteen days with a scrape interval of fifteen seconds across too many high-cardinality labels. A pod-level label on a metric with per-request identity was the main offender.

aws eks update-kubeconfig --name metabare-dev --region eu-west-1
Updated context arn:aws:eks:eu-west-1:000000000000:cluster/metabare-dev in /home/user/.kube/config

kubectl get nodes
error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)

The IAM principal was not in the cluster access entries. Creating an access entry with the AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy fixed it.

Grafana dashboard showing queue depth, node count and GPU utilisation on one aligned timeline. The queue rises sharply after a batch upload, a node appears roughly ninety seconds later, GPU utilisation climbs to full, the queue drains, and the node disappears.

The KEDA ScaledObject would not scale from zero. minReplicaCount was set to 1, so there was always one pod running and the scale-to-zero claim was not true.

Setting minReplicaCount to 0 and using the SQS queue length trigger with an activation threshold made it genuinely zero when idle.

Architecture diagram: an upload API writing to object storage, an event fanning out to two queues, CPU workers doing extraction on one and GPU workers doing image encoding on the other, both writing to a shared search index backed by the same object store.

The Lambda function timed out after fifteen minutes. It was iterating over every object in a bucket with a ListObjectsV2 paginator and calling HeadObject for each one.

Eleven million objects at roughly forty milliseconds per head request was never going to finish. Switching to S3 Inventory turned it into a nightly Parquet read.

helm upgrade --install kube-prometheus-stack prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack --version 65.1.0
Error: UPGRADE FAILED: cannot patch "prometheus-kube-prometheus-prometheus" with kind Prometheus: admission webhook denied the request

The CRDs were from an older chart version. Helm does not upgrade CRDs on its own; they had to be applied manually first.

Terraform state was locked by a run that had been killed. 

Error acquiring the state lock: ConditionalCheckFailedException
Lock Info:
  ID:        7f3a1c2e-9b44
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Created:   2026-04-11 09:14:02

terraform force-unlock 7f3a1c2e-9b44 released it, after confirming no apply was actually running.

Note on embedding models: the query prefix matters. BGE is trained with an instruction on the query side only. Encoding indexed passages with the same prefix measurably degraded retrieval, and omitting it on queries did too. The two paths need separate code.

The RDS instance ran out of burst credits. IOPS fell off a cliff at 03:40 and stayed at baseline for the rest of the night while the nightly batch job ran.

gp2 credit accumulation depends on volume size. The fix was moving to gp3 with provisioned IOPS decoupled from capacity.

OCR on terminal screenshots was much worse than on console screenshots. Anti-aliased white-on-black monospace text at a small point size confused the recogniser badly, with l and 1 and I frequently swapped.

Upscaling the image before recognition helped more than any model change.

docker build failed on the final stage.

COPY --from=builder /app/.venv /app/.venv
failed to compute cache key: failed to calculate checksum: "/app/.venv": not found

The builder stage had installed into a different path because the working directory was set after the install step, not before.

Cost per thousand screenshots processed on g4dn.xlarge Spot came out lower than on g5.xlarge Spot for small batches, because the g5 spent proportionally more of its billed lifetime starting up than working.

For a ten thousand image backfill the ranking reversed.

The vector search returned nothing at all for every query. The namespace had rows and the vector-only path worked fine.

Adding a text field to the request turned a working query into a 500. The namespace had no full-text index, and one has to be built explicitly after the first write.
